About: Thin Lens & Lens-Maker's Equation

Source

Topic
Geometrical Optics — thin lens formula & lens-maker's equation (NCERT Class 12).
Concept
The focal length is not a free parameter — it is set by the glass (n) and the surface curvature (R), and once known, one equation places every image.
Serves
Reading a ray diagram; the NCERT Cartesian sign convention (1/v − 1/u = 1/f, m = v/u — note the minus, unlike the mirror formula); the real→virtual transition at |u| = f; the magnifying glass (|u| < f).
Inquiry
Place the object at |u| = 2f — predict where the image lands. Then walk it inward through the focal point.
Misconception target
“A virtual image is not really there.” You see it perfectly well — but no light converges there, so it cannot be caught on a screen.

Guided Inquiry

1. The object sits at |u| = 2f. Where does the image land?

The focal length here is f = 0.20 m (from R = 0.20 m, n = 1.5), so the object is at u = −0.40 m. The rays stop at the lens until you commit. Predict.

2. Walk the object inward. What happens to the image?

Slowly drag the Object distance u slider left, from |u| = 0.40 m in toward 0.20 m (= f). Watch the image arrow on the right.

It races outward — the image runs away from the lens far faster than the object approaches it, and grows.

3. The object now sits exactly on F (|u| = f). What does the picture do?

u = −0.20 m, and f = 0.20 m. Predict before the rays leave the lens.

4. Now |u| < f (u = −0.10 m). A friend says “a virtual image isn't really there.”

The object is inside the focal point — this is the magnifying glass. Judge the claim, then commit to see what the rays do.

5. Free exploration

All three controls are yours. Try: (a) same glass (n = 1.5) with a fatter radius R = 0.24 m — f grows. (b) Denser glass (n = 1.6) with R = 0.24 m — f is 0.20 m again: a fatter radius offset by denser glass. The focal length is not a slider — it is computed from R and n. Two formulae, one mechanism.

Thin lens formula (NCERT)
Cartesian signs, measured from the optical centre with light going left → right: u < 0 for a real object in front of the lens; v > 0 for a real image on the far side, v < 0 for a virtual image on the same side; f > 0 converging. Note the MINUS — the mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with m = −v/u, the lens formula is not. m > 0 upright, m < 0 inverted; |m| > 1 enlarged.
Lens-maker's equation (equiconvex: r₁ = +R, r₂ = −R)
Power P = 1/f, in dioptres when f is in metres. f is not a slider — it comes from (n, R) through this equation, then places the image through the formula on the left.

01

At a glance

A convex lens gathers the light from an object into an image. The sim builds the lens from its glass and its curvature, then lets one equation place the image.

What you'll learn

  • How the focal length f follows from the refractive index n and the radius of curvature R.
  • How the signs of u, v and f describe where an image sits and what kind it is.
  • How the image distance and the magnification change as the object moves past the focal point.
The bench: an object at distance u from a lens, with the focal points F and twice that distance, 2F, marked on both sides.

What's on screen

  • Lens: the teal line, with its focal length f above it.
  • F and 2F: amber dots at one focal length, grey dots at two, on both sides.
  • Object and image: the white arrow, and a purple arrow that is dashed when the image is virtual.
  • Three rays: blue 1, pink 2 and amber 3, with a legend at the top right.
  • Labels and readouts: u, v and m on the bench, and the panel on the right.
See itPut the object at u = −0.500 m with the opening lens, R = 0.200 m and n = 1.50. Watch for: the object arrow on the left, f = 0.200 m above the lens, and numbered rays crossing it.

Fixed: a thin equiconvex lens in air, so the two faces have equal radius R. There is no control for f, because the lens fixes it.

03

The glass and the curvature set the focal length

The lens has two faces of equal radius R, bulging outward, in glass of index n. The lens-maker's equation gives its focal length f. The two faces have radii +R and −R:

1/f = (n − 1)(1/R − 1/(−R)) = 2(n − 1)/R
So f = R / (2(n − 1)).
  • A larger R gives a longer f. A larger n gives a shorter f.
  • The power of the lens is P = 1/f, in dioptres when f is in metres. At the opening values f = 0.200 m, so P = 5 D.
  • The lens is treated as thin, so its thickness is ignored.

Different pairs of R and n can give the same f. A fatter radius in denser glass can focus just like a tighter radius in lighter glass.

See itSet R = 0.240 m with n = 1.60. Watch for: f = 0.200 m above the lens, the same as at the opening values, even though R is larger.
04

The lens equation places the image

Distances are measured from the centre of the lens, with light travelling left to right (the NCERT Cartesian convention). The equation and the magnification are

1/v − 1/u = 1/f    m = v/u
u: object distance. v: image distance. f: focal length.
  • u < 0 for a real object in front of the lens. f > 0 for this converging lens.
  • v > 0: the image is on the far side. v < 0: it is on the same side as the object.
  • m < 0: inverted. m > 0: upright. |m| > 1: enlarged.
  • The mirror formula is 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with m = −v/u. The lens equation has the minus sign instead.

Ray 1 runs parallel to the axis and leaves through the far F. Ray 2 goes straight through the lens centre. Ray 3 aims along the line through the near F and leaves parallel to the axis. They meet at the tip of the image.

See itPut the object at u = −0.600 m. Watch for: v = +0.300 m and m = −0.50, with the three rays meeting at an arrow on the far side.
05

An object at 2f gives an image at 2f

Put the object at u = −2f in 1/v = 1/f + 1/u:

1/v = 1/f − 1/(2f) = 1/(2f)
So v = +2f, and m = v/u = −1.
  • The image is real, on the far side, at the same distance 2f as the object, and inverted.
  • It is exactly the same size as the object, since |m| = 1.
  • This symmetric point separates enlarged images from diminished ones.

At the opening values f = 0.200 m, so the object at u = −0.400 m gives v = +0.400 m. Beyond 2f the image is smaller than the object. Between f and 2f it is larger.

See itUse the opening lens with the object at u = −0.400 m. Watch for: v = +0.400 m and m = −1.00, with an inverted purple arrow as tall as the white one.
06

As the object nears F the image runs away

Between 2f and f, 1/v = 1/f − 1/|u|. As |u| shrinks toward f, the right side shrinks toward zero, so v grows without limit. With f = 0.200 m:

|u|vm
0.400 m0.400 m−1
0.300 m0.600 m−2
0.250 m1.000 m−4
0.220 m2.200 m−10

Moving the object 0.100 m closer, from 0.400 m to 0.300 m, moves the image 0.200 m farther away. At exactly |u| = f, 1/v = 0: the rays leave the lens parallel and meet nowhere, so the image is at infinity. A small bulb at F gives a parallel beam, as in a torch.

See itSet the object exactly on F, at u = −0.200 m. Watch for: image at ∞ on the bench, v = ∞ below it, and the rays leaving the lens parallel.
07

Inside F the image is virtual, upright and enlarged

For |u| < f, 1/v = 1/f − 1/|u| is negative, so v is negative. The image sits on the same side as the object. At u = −0.100 m with f = 0.200 m, 1/v = 5 − 10 = −5, so v = −0.200 m and m = v/u = +2.

  • The rays leave the lens still spreading apart, so they never meet on the far side.
  • Traced backward, they appear to come from one point. The sim draws these backward extensions dashed, and the image arrow dashed too.
  • No light actually reaches that point, so a screen placed there stays blank. Your eye still sees the image, because it is the rays entering the eye that matter.

A magnifying glass works this way: the object sits inside f, and the eye looks at the upright, enlarged virtual image.

See itPut the object inside F, at u = −0.100 m. Watch for: a dashed virtual image arrow on the object's side, v = −0.200 m and m = +2.00.
08

Where it matters

  • Cameras and projectors. A real image can be caught on a sensor or a screen. A projector holds the slide just outside f, so the image lands far away and is large.
  • Magnifiers. A magnifying glass or a reading lens works with the object inside f, giving an upright, enlarged virtual image.
  • Parallel beams. A small lamp at the focal point of a lens leaves it as a nearly parallel beam, as in a torch or a lighthouse.
  • Spectacles. An optician quotes the power P = 1/f in dioptres. A lens with f = 0.200 m is +5 D.
09

Summary

In one line. The glass and the curvature fix f, and f with the object distance fixes where the image lands, how big it is and which way up.

Key points

  • f = R / (2(n − 1)) for this lens, and P = 1/f.
  • 1/v − 1/u = 1/f and m = v/u, with u < 0 for a real object.
  • Where |u| sits relative to f and 2f decides what kind of image forms.

Common mix-ups

  • "A virtual image is not really there." You see it clearly. No light converges there, so no screen can catch it.
  • "The lens equation is the mirror formula." The lens has 1/v − 1/u = 1/f with m = v/u. A mirror has 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with m = −v/u.
  • "Focal length is a setting." Here f is worked out from R and n.

Things to try on your own

  • Set R = 0.240 m with n = 1.50, then find the u that gives an image of the same size.
  • Find another pair of R and n, with R = 0.300 m, that gives f = 0.200 m.
  • Keep u = −0.300 m and raise n from 1.50 to 1.90. Say what m will do, then read it.
